gist: Opens Chapter III, Atwood's annotated presentation of the Golden Treatise of Hermes (Section First). The main text is Hermes speaking. Atwood's footnotes, often relaying 'the Scholiast', decode its images: the elements, the division of the Water, the Weights, decoction and tincture, Argent vive, the vulture and crow, the Stone, the moist fire, and the agents. They also stress secrecy and the moral and divine requirements placed on the operator.

notes.point: Chapter heading: Chapter 3 presents 'The Golden Treatise of Hermes Trismegistus, Concerning the Physical Secret of the Philosopher's Stone', in seven sections; Section First begins.

Hermes says he experimented for long years and spared no labour of mind, yet obtained the science and art by the inspiration of the living God alone, who opened it to him as His servant. To those able by reason to judge truth, God gave power to arbitrate, but to none 'occasion of delinquency'.

Three things are necessary for the Hermetic science: study, experience and divine benediction. Each depends on the others: study is needed for the theory, and the theory for entering into 'the central experience', which in the Universal Spirit is not found without God.

Without theoretic knowledge and a right principle to begin with, many have exhausted themselves experimenting, and even with the right theory they go back and forth in the work. Geber is cited: whoever knows the principles and the way of generation according to the intention of nature is a very short way from completion, unlike one with no 'true root' for his intention. The passage is garbled and repeated in the source.
Hermes discloses the matter only for fear of the day of judgment and the loss of his soul if he concealed it. It is a debt to the faithful, as the Father of the faith bestowed it on him.

Atwood: conscience moved Hermes to disclose, but only in terms the studious could understand and follow. He never addresses the ignorant, lest the teaching be abused. He addresses the 'predestined sons of wisdom', already initiated, to guide them further into the practice.

Hermes: the ancients did not seek knowledge of the four elements corporally or imprudently. The elements are found through patience, according to their causes and occult operation. Their operation is occult because nothing is done unless it is compounded, and nothing is perfected unless the colours are thoroughly passed through and accomplished.

Atwood calls this a 'premonitory opening' of the work, which Hermes calls knowledge of the elements. The elements are not to be understood in the common way, but, as the Scholiast says, 'spiritually and wisely'. The properties of the Universal Spirit are hidden in all existence and understood only by its own intimate analysis and 'introverted light'.

Atwood renders Hermes' 'compounded' as 'decompounded': nothing is done unless the matter is decompounded. In its natural state the subject carries heterogeneous images and superfluities that stop its progress, and these must be wholly discharged. The adepts say this is impossible without the theory of their arcanum, which shows the medium by which the radical element is discovered and set free.

Hermes: the ancients divided the Water into four substances, 'one to two, and three to one'. One third part is colour, that is, a coagulating moisture; the two third waters are the Weights of the Wise. A recipe follows: humidity 1.5 oz; Meridian Redness (soul of gold) a fourth part, 0.5 oz; citrine Seyre 0.5 oz; Auripigment half, 'which are eight', making three ounces. The vine of the wise is drawn forth in three and its wine perfected in thirty.

Atwood: the philosophic water is divided into four parts or 'hypostatic relations', called elements. The one, divided, produces two, which act as agent and patient in the ethereal world. From their conjunction three appear as body, soul and spirit. Working together in the unity of the same spirit, these beget all things and give birth to the whole substratal nature.
The Scholiast says Hermes divides the colours into two threes, three red spirits and three white, all growing from the same water and resolving into it again.

This water, or mercury of the adepts, holds its own good sulfur or vital flame, so all things can be perfected out of mercury. Whoever adds his weights to nature's, doubling mercury and tripling sulfur, will quickly bring the work to good, then better, then best.

Adepts give the proportional working of the matter on its parts under perplexing forms and measures. The Scholiast says Hermes' terms (humidity, southern redness, soul of gold, seyre, citrine, auripigment, vine and wine) mean only that the spirit is distilled seven times. After the eighth distillation, the force of the fire turns it into ashes or a most subtle powder that resists fire by its purity. Eight parts equal three ounces because the one part is divided into two and three parts are added to each; these are the true philosophic proportions, the Weights of the Wise.
Hermes: decoction lessens the matter and the tincture increases it. Luna is diminished after fifteen days and increased in the third. This is the beginning and the end.

Atwood: this means the decrease and increase of the ethereal light, the 'passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven'. Its changes run parallel to the moon's, so the philosopher names it by analogy with the moon. Some divide the operation into two parts. The first, decoction, dissolves the matter and discharges its impurities by rule until, near annihilation and free of every form attracting it from outside, the matter prepares to restore itself through an inbred revolutionary force (Democritus' fable of Proteus). The Second Work, a continuation of the First, perfects the 'newly informed embryo' and multiplies its vivific light. In these few words Hermes covers the whole process of working the Spirit.
Hermes: he has declared what was concealed, since the work is 'both with you and about you'. Taking what is within and fixed, you can have it in earth or sea.

Atwood: enquirers should leave the 'beaten road of experiment' and seek to know within themselves the substance of the Universal Nature, in which all beings live unconsciously and which stays hidden in the natural order of generation. Gross elementary bodies cannot reveal their true original unless reduced into it. In the same way, what is sown in man (the catholic germ of his existence) is not quickened unless it dies.

Atwood continues: what is within, the causal light, must be drawn out by art and fixed. What is without, the sensual spirit of life, must be made flexible and hidden. Only then can reason enter into 'that Identity' by which the powers of the Universal Nature are revealed and understood from within. She defers further comment.

Hermes: keep your Argent vive, prepared and coagulated in the innermost chamber; this is the Mercury spoken of concerning the residual earth. He says he has disclosed every hidden thing and the greatest secret, and the hearer should search his words. The vulture on the mountain cries: 'I am the White of the Black, and the Red of the White, and the Citrine of the Red'.

The Scholiast: 'our Mercury' is philosophic, fiery, vital and running. It mixes with all metals and separates from them again. It is prepared and coagulated in the innermost chamber of life, found where metals grow, 'in the ultimate axle of each created life'. This argent vive is the residue of the philosophic earth after separation and should be kept safe. If the mercurial spirit is brought to ashes or burnt by its own fire, it is an incomparable treasure that both generates the Stone and is born of it. It converts other metals into silver and gold and gives them tincture and fixity.

Atwood cites the Divine Teacher's 'pearls before swine' and the Scripture comparisons of some men to dogs, wolves and foxes. Such men are unfit for the Causal Knowledge: handling nature's 'powerful machine' for selfish ends, they would overturn the order of final causes. Hermes therefore leaves the Mystery to unfold through study and faithful experiment, so that searching prepares the mind to recognise the truth when found. Atwood will explore the 'Intellectual Ground' later.

The Scholiast: the vulture is the newborn quintessential spirit, or Proteus. The mountain is a fit vessel set in a well-built philosophic furnace walled with fire. The vulture holds all of nature's virtues in potential. Spinning rapidly about his axis, he makes the light visible without refraction, in all its colours.

Hermes: the chief principle of the art is the Crow, which flies without wings in the black of night and the clear of day. The tincture is taken from the bitterness in its throat, the red comes from its body, and a pure water is taken from its back. In the caverns of the metals lies the stone: venerable, splendid in colour, 'a mind sublime, and an open sea'. Put the matter into a moist fire and boil it so its heat increases, destroying the dryness of the incombustible nature until the radix appears. Then extract the redness and the light part until a third part remains.

The vulture and the crow are one thing in different states. When the Spirit of life is active and devouring it is the vulture; when obscured and passive, the crow. The vulture is the first sublimed quintessence, not yet perfected. The crow is the infancy of the work in which the revived spirit unites with its solar ferment. Night is putrefaction and day is resurrection to comparative purity. It flies without wings because the fixed spirit carries it. The throat's bitterness signals the death of the first life, from which the soul is drawn out; this is also the red living tincture taken from the body. The thin water is the viscous humidity made by dissolution, which dissolves all metals at the root and reduces them to their first ens, water. A Latin verse from Atalanta Fugiens is cited.

Atwood: Hermes again excludes the unintelligent while identifying the matter as 'mens sublimes et mare patens'. 'Hidden in the caverns of the metals' means in the central motion of the mineral life, where the spirit first coagulates and takes concrete form. The adepts call it a stone and a true mineral petrification. Alphidus and Arnold are cited: it is 'a stone and no stone', spirit, soul and body, which dissolves, coagulates or flies as it is made to, being volatile and clear as a tear.

Adepts name many operations (sublimation, calcination, inceration, fixation), but all fall under the first, sublimation, rightly understood. Repeated over and over, Hermetic sublimation causes many changes that carry different names but have one source. It is not ordinary chemical sublimation, a mere lifting of the subject to the top of the vessel. It changes and improves the matter each time, pushing life to its utmost vigour to save itself from death and total disseveration. The nature, origin and artificial excitation of the philosophic fire are deferred.

Hermes: philosophers are called envious not because they withhold truth from the just or wise, but because they withhold it from the ignorant and vicious, who lack self-control and benevolence, lest these grow powerful in evil. Philosophers answer to God for this. The matter is called the Stone, and also the feminine of magnesia, the hen, white spittle, volatile milk and incombustible ash, to hide it from the inept. To the wise it is signified by one epithet, the Philosopher's Stone. Enclose and keep in this sea the fire and the heavenly Flyer until the last moment of his exit. Never open this Stone to the foolish.

Warnings to secrecy are frequent and stringent among adepts. Lully's Thesaurus gives an oath of damnation for revealing. Norton's verse says the science must stay secret because one evil man could destroy Christian peace and pull down rightful kings, and the peril falls on the teacher.

The matter has many perplexing names, but in its concrete form it is properly called the Stone, and Hermes includes all its 'multinominal ingredients' in it. In its flowing, humid state it is the sea of the wise, passive to every impression of the light. According to the Scholiast, the fire and the heavenly bird are the external and internal agents of the work, by either of which the matter is conserved and nourished to the end.
Hermes: he received nothing he did not return, and never failed to honour Him.

The adepts say the chief art of operating lies in friendship, gratitude and reciprocity of benefaction. No man can carry out the Hermetic artifice alone, for reasons to be explained later. A verse after Arnold says no man may mortify Mercury except with his brother's knowledging, and that Hermes first declared this.

Hermes: this is the concealed Stone of many colours, born in one colour. With God's favour it escapes the greatest diseases and drives out all sorrow and harm. It leads from darkness to light, from the wilderness to a secure dwelling, and from poverty to fortune.

Atwood: Hermes covertly marks the consummate union of the purified spirit with its 'course' as the cornerstone of his philosophy. That 'tincture of many dyes' renews itself when dissolved and survives its own dying until its final cause is accomplished. It is the elixir of Light from the central essence, set free, and is said to prolong life and cure disease, moral indulgence and physical defects.

method.veiled: study, experience, and the divine benediction
method.plain: The operator needs study (for theory), practical experience, and God's blessing. Each depends on the others, and the 'central experience' is not reached without God.
method.basis: I.3 n1 states this directly; I.3 ¶3 (Hermes) attributes his knowledge to 'the inspiration of the living God alone'.

method.veiled: a true root whereon to found his intention
method.plain: Before experimenting, the operator must know the principles and how generation works according to nature's intention; without that, experimenting is wasted effort.
method.basis: I.3 n2: 'Without theoretic knowledge and a right principle to begin with, many have wearied themselves in experimenting'; Geber is cited to the same effect.

method.veiled: the knowledge of the four elements of the ancient philosophers
method.plain: The 'elements' are not physical substances. They are the properties of the Universal Spirit, present hidden in all existence, and known only through that spirit's own inward analysis.
method.basis: I.3 n4: 'not corporally but spiritually and wisely; for the properties of the Universal Spirit are abstrusely included in all existence'. I.3 n5: the four parts of the philosophic water 'are called elements'.

method.veiled: nothing is done except it be compounded
method.plain: Atwood reads this as: nothing is done until the matter is broken down ('decompounded') and stripped of the foreign images and excess it carries in its natural state.
method.basis: I.3 n4: 'nothing is done except that the matter be decompounded'. See ambiguities, since Hermes' word is 'compounded'.

method.veiled: many heterogeneous images and superfluities adhering to this subject in its natural state
method.plain: In its ordinary state the subject is cluttered with foreign images and excess matter that block progress. These must be fully discharged, which the adepts say cannot be done without their theory.

method.veiled: the radical element is discovered and set free to the accomplishment of its inclusive law
method.plain: The aim of the purification is to uncover and free the root element of the subject so that it can fulfil its own law.

method.veiled: it is not perfected unless the colours be thoroughly passed and accomplished
method.plain: The work goes through a series of colour stages, and it is not complete until every one has been fully passed.
method.basis: I.3 ¶9: the vulture says 'I am the White of the Black, and the Red of the White, and the Citrine of the Red'. I.3 n5: three red and three white spirits from one water. I.3 n11: the light made manifest 'in every variety of its coloring'. I.3 ¶13: the Stone 'of many colours; which is born in one colour'.

method.veiled: the division that was made upon the Water, by the ancient philosophers, separates it into four substances; one to two, and three to one
method.plain: One philosophic water differentiates in stages. The one splits into two, acting as agent and patient; their union produces three (body, soul and spirit), which work together as one spirit to generate all things.
method.basis: I.3 n5: 'the one part, being divided, produces two, which are as agent and patient in the ethereal world ... three are said to be made manifest as body, soul, and spirit'.

method.veiled: the one third part of which is colour, that is to say --- a coagulating moisture
method.plain: The text equates the 'colour' part of the Water with a moisture that coagulates (sets or solidifies). It gives no further explanation.
method.basis: I.3 ¶6 gives the identity ('that is to say').

method.veiled: the two third waters are the Weights of the Wise
method.plain: The 'Weights of the Wise' are the true philosophic proportions: the one part divided into two, with three parts added to each.
method.basis: I.3 n6: 'the one part is divided into two, to each of which there are added three parts, which are the true philosophic proportions called also by Hermes the Weights of the Wise'.

method.veiled: to add thy weights to the weights of nature, to double mercury and triple sulfur
method.plain: The operator adds his own proportions to nature's, doubling the mercury and tripling the sulfur, and the work then advances from good to better to best. The text does not say concretely what 'doubling' and 'tripling' are.
method.basis: I.3 n5 (the instruction itself); I.3 n6 for the Weights as proportions of one into two plus three parts.

method.veiled: Take of the humidity an ounce and a half, and of the Meridian Redness, that is the soul of gold, a fourth part
method.plain: The quantities in this recipe are not literal measures. They encode a repeated distillation of the spirit: seven distillations, after which the eighth turns it by the fire's force into ashes, a very fine powder that resists fire.
method.basis: I.3 n6: these distinctions 'have no other signification ... but that the spirit should be seven times distilled, which after the eighth distillation is converted by force of the fire into ashes'.

method.veiled: the vine of the wise is drawn forth in three, and the wine thereof is perfected in thirty
method.plain: This is part of the same coded proportional distillation described in n6. The text gives no separate meaning for 'three' and 'thirty'.
method.basis: I.3 n6 includes 'the cine of the philosophers and their wine' in the terms that signify only the sevenfold distillation.

method.veiled: Decoction lessens the matter, but the tincture augments it
method.plain: There are two phases. First, decoction dissolves the matter and drives out its impurities until it is nearly annihilated and free of every outward form, at which point an inborn force makes it restore itself. Second (the 'Second Work'), the newly formed embryo is perfected and its life-giving light multiplied.

method.veiled: Luna after fifteen days is diminished; and in the third, she is augmented
method.plain: The decrease and increase of an inner 'ethereal light', the passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven, which waxes and wanes like the moon during the work.
method.basis: I.3 n7: 'Understand here the diminution and increase of that ethereal light, which is the passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven'. The day-counts are not explained.

method.veiled: being at length on the verge of annihilation; i.e., freed from every exteriorly attracting form
method.plain: The low point of the dissolution: stripped of all outward attachments, the matter turns and rebuilds itself by its own inner power.

method.veiled: the work is both with you and about you
method.plain: The work is done in the enquirer: one must know within oneself the substance of the Universal Nature in which all beings live without knowing it, instead of following ordinary outward experiment.
method.basis: I.3 n8: enquirers should 'forsake the beaten road of experiment, and seek to know intrinsical within themselves the substance of that Universal Nature'.

method.veiled: taking what is within and fixed
method.plain: The inner causal light is drawn out by art and fixed (made stable). The outer, sensual spirit of life is made flexible and hidden. Only then can reason reach the 'Identity' in which the powers of the Universal Nature are known from within.
method.basis: I.3 n8: 'That which is within, viz., the causal light, must be drawn forth by art and fixed; and that which is without, viz., the sensual spirit of life must be made flexible and occultated'.

method.veiled: is not quickened except it die
method.plain: The germ of a person's existence must pass through a death before it comes alive. Similarly, gross bodies show their true original only when reduced back into it.

method.veiled: Keep, therefore, thy Argent vive, which is prepared in the innermost chamber in which it is coagulated
method.plain: The essential substance is 'our Mercury': a fiery, vital, mobile spirit prepared and solidified in the innermost chamber of life ('the ultimate axle of each created life'). It is what is left of the philosophic earth after separation, and it must be kept.
method.basis: I.3 n9: 'It is prepared in the innermost chamber of life ... the residuum of the philosophic earth after the separation, keep it safely'.

method.veiled: If you have brought your mercurial spirit to ashes or burnt it by its own fire
method.plain: Reduce the mercurial spirit to ash by its own fire and you have the treasure that both generates the Stone and is born of it, and that gives tincture and fixity to metals.

method.veiled: the vulture standing upon the mountain crieth out with a loud voice, I am the White of the Black, and the Red of the White, and the Citrine of the Red
method.plain: The vulture is the newborn quintessential spirit, active and devouring. Its cry names a sequence of colours (black, white, red, citrine) that it carries in itself and shows as the work goes on.
method.basis: I.3 n11: vulture = 'the new born quintessential spirit or Proteus', making light manifest 'in every variety of its coloring'. I.3 n12: vulture = Spirit of life 'active and devouring'. The colour sequence itself is not glossed.

method.veiled: the mountain upon which the vulture stands
method.plain: A suitable vessel set in a well-built philosophic furnace, surrounded by a wall of fire.

method.veiled: as in rapid evolution he passes about his axis, making the light manifest without refraction in every variety of its coloring
method.plain: The newborn spirit turns rapidly about its own axis and shows its light directly in every colour.
method.basis: I.3 n11 gives the image but no further gloss; linked to the colour stages of I.3 ¶5 and ¶9.

method.veiled: the chief principle of the art is the Crow
method.plain: The crow is the same spirit as the vulture in a darker, passive state. It belongs to the beginning of the work, in which the revived spirit is united with its solar ferment.
method.basis: I.3 n12: 'The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate ... the crow is also in the infancy of that work wherein the revivified spirit is united with its solar ferment'.

method.veiled: in the blackness of the night and clearness of the day
method.plain: Night = the putrefaction (rotting/decomposition) of the spirit. Day = its resurrection to comparative purity.

method.veiled: flies without wings
method.plain: The volatile spirit rises because the fixed spirit carries it, not by its own power.
method.basis: I.3 n12: 'IT flies without wings, being borne and carried by the fixed spirit'.

method.veiled: From the bitterness existing in the throat, the tincture is taken; the red goes forth from his body
method.plain: The death of the first life, from which the soul is drawn out. That soul is the red, living tincture taken from the body.
method.basis: I.3 n12: 'the bitterness existing in the throat occultly indicates the death of the first life, whence the soul is ediced; which is also the red and living tincture taken from the body'.

method.veiled: from his back is taken a pure water
method.plain: The viscous humidity produced by the dissolution. It dissolves all metals at the root and returns them to their first ens, water.
method.basis: I.3 n12: 'the thin water is the viscous humidity made by the dissolution which radically dissolves all metals'.

method.veiled: In the caverns of the metals there is hidden the stone
method.plain: The matter lies in the central motion of mineral life, where the spirit first coagulates and takes concrete form.
method.basis: I.3 n13: 'It is hidden in the caverns of the metals; that is to say, in the central motion of the mineral life'.

method.veiled: a mind sublime, and an open sea
method.plain: Names for the philosophic matter itself. 'Sea' fits its flowing, humid state, open to every impression of the light; 'mind' suggests the matter has an intellectual or spiritual nature.
method.basis: I.3 n13: Hermes 'identifies the philosophic matter, calling it mens sublimes et mare patens'. I.3 n16: 'In its flowing, humid state it is called the sea of the wise, passive to all impression and influences of the light'. The 'mind' reading is not glossed in the text.

method.veiled: a stone and no stone, spirit, soul, and body
method.plain: The matter is called a stone, yet is not an ordinary stone. It is spirit, soul and body together and does whatever it is made to: dissolve, coagulate or fly.
method.basis: I.3 n13, citing Arnold.

method.veiled: Put the matter into a moist fire, therefore, and cause it to boil in order that its heat may be augmented
method.plain: Heat the matter in a moist medium and keep raising the heat until the dryness of its fire-resisting nature is broken down and its root (radix) appears. Atwood groups all such operations under 'Hermetic sublimation' and does not yet explain the 'moist fire'.
method.basis: I.3 ¶10 (literal instruction); I.3 n14 says all operations fall under sublimation and defers the philosophic fire ('we may more effectively inquire hereafter'); I.3 n4 'radical element is discovered and set free'.

method.veiled: then extract the redness and the light part, till the third part remains
method.plain: After the root appears, the red and light portions are drawn off until a third remains. The text does not say what the red and light portions or the remaining third are.
method.basis: I.3 ¶10 only; I.3 n12 links 'the red' to the tincture or soul taken from the body, which may bear on 'redness'.

method.veiled: the Hermetic sublimation, repeatedly operated over and over again
method.plain: One operation repeated many times. Each round changes and improves the matter, driving its life to full vigour to avoid death and dissolution. Sublimation, calcination, inceration and fixation are names for its effects, not separate processes. It is not ordinary chemical sublimation.

method.veiled: the ignorant and vicious, who are without self-control and benevolence
method.plain: The art is kept from people who lack self-control and goodwill, because it would make them powerful in evil. Only the just and the wise may receive it.
method.basis: I.3 ¶11; I.3 n10 (such men 'unfit to be admitted to the Causal Knowledge'); I.3 n15.

method.veiled: the feminine of magnesia, or the hen, or the white spittle, or the volatile milk, the incombustible ash
method.plain: These are all cover-names for the one matter, the Stone, chosen to hide it from the unworthy.
method.basis: I.3 ¶11: 'this matter I call the Stone; but it is also named ... in order that it may be hidden from the inept'. I.3 n16.

method.veiled: Include, therefore, and conserve in this sea, the fire, and the heavenly Flyer, to the latest moment of his exit
method.plain: Keep the external and internal agents (the fire and the heavenly bird) enclosed with the matter in its fluid state (the 'sea') to the very end, since they conserve and nourish it.
method.basis: I.3 n16: 'In its flowing, humid state it is called the sea of the wise ... By the fire and heavenly bird are dignified ... the external and internal agents in the Hermetic work, by either of which it is conserved and nourished to the end'. Which agent is which is ambiguous.

method.veiled: In friendship, gratitude, and reciprocity of benefaction, say the adepts, consists the chief art of operating with their matter
method.plain: The work depends on friendship, gratitude and mutual benefit, and no one can perform it alone.
method.basis: I.3 n17: 'no man, for reasons hereafter explicable, can operate the Hermetic artifice alone'. I.3 ¶12 (Hermes returned all he received).

method.veiled: There may noe man Mercury mortify, But it be with his brother’s knowledging
method.plain: Mercury cannot be 'mortified' (killed or fixed) except with another person's knowledge or participation.
method.basis: I.3 n17 cites this verse right after saying no man can operate the artifice alone. 'Mortify' is read through I.3 n12 and n8 on the death of the first life; the exact role of the 'brother' is not stated.
method.voice: QUOTED: Arnolde of the New Towne

method.veiled: Hermes leaves the Mystery thus, therefore, to unfold itself through study and faithful experiment
method.plain: The teaching is left incomplete on purpose, so that patient searching trains the student's mind to recognise the truth when found.

method.veiled: the concealed Stone of many colours; which is born in one colour
method.plain: The finished Stone comes from one source and passes through many colours. It removes disease and sorrow and leads from darkness to light.

method.veiled: The consummate union of the purified spirit with its course
method.plain: The goal is the complete union of the purified spirit with its origin or course. The result is a self-renewing tincture, the 'elixir of Light' from the central essence, said to prolong life and cure bodily disease, moral indulgence and physical defects.
method.basis: I.3 n18. 'course' may be a misprint; see ambiguities.

method.veiled: this water or mercury of the adepts has, within itself, its own good sulfur, or vital flame
method.plain: The philosophic water holds its own active principle (sulfur, vital flame), so it contains everything needed to perfect all things.
method.basis: I.3 n5: 'thou mayest perfect all things out of mercury'.

terms.meaning: The art Hermes received by divine inspiration. It needs study, experience and divine benediction, and cannot be performed alone.

quotes.text: There are three things said to be necessary for the attainment of the Hermetic science: viz., study, experience, and the divine benediction

terms.meaning: A spirit whose properties are hidden in all existence and understood only by its own intimate analysis. The central experience 'in the Universal Spirit' is not found without God.

quotes.text: the properties of the Universal Spirit are abstrusely included in all existence, and to be understood only by its own intimate analysis and introverted light

terms.meaning: Not physical bodies but spiritual properties. They are the four parts or 'hypostatic relations' into which the philosophic water is divided.

equivalences.with: four parts or hypostatic relations of the philosophic water
equivalences.quote: The philosophic water then, being divided into four parts or hypostatic relations, they are called elements.

quotes.text: non corporaliter, as the Scholiast explains, sed spiritualiter et sapienter, --- not corporally but spiritually and wisely

terms.meaning: Atwood's reading of Hermes' 'compounded': breaking the matter down and clearing away the foreign images and excess that cling to it in its natural state.

quotes.text: nothing is done except that the matter be decompounded

terms.meaning: The root element of the subject, which the work uncovers and sets free. In ¶10, the 'radix' appears once the dryness of the incombustible nature is destroyed.

equivalences.quote: reduces them into their first ens, or water

quotes.text: the medium by which the radical element is discovered and set free to the accomplishment of its inclusive law
until the radix shall appear

terms.meaning: The single source substance. It divides into one, two and three (agent and patient; body, soul and spirit) and so begets all things. The red and white spirits grow from it and resolve into it. In its flowing, humid state it is the 'sea of the wise', passive to the light.

equivalences.quote: this water or mercury of the adepts has, within itself, its own good sulfur, or vital flame
In its flowing, humid state it is called the sea of the wise

quotes.text: the division that was made upon the Water, by the ancient philosophers, separates it into four substances; one to two, and three to one

terms.meaning: The two produced when the one is divided, in the ethereal world. The Scholiast also says the mercurial treasure makes metals 'agent and patient'.

quotes.text: the one part, being divided, produces two, which are as agent and patient in the ethereal world

terms.meaning: The three that appear from the union of agent and patient. Working in the unity of one spirit, they beget all things. Arnold also calls the Stone 'spirit, soul, and body'.

quotes.text: three are said to be made manifest as body, soul, and spirit, which cooperating together in the unity of the same spirit, beget all things

variants: three red spirits and three white
terms.meaning: In ¶6, the one-third part of the Water, identified as a coagulating moisture. In general, the stages the work must fully pass through. The colours divide into three red spirits and three white, all from one water.

equivalences.quote: the one third part of which is colour, that is to say --- a coagulating moisture

quotes.text: it is not perfected unless the colours be thoroughly passed and accomplished
Hermes divides into two threes, i.e., into three red spirits and three white

terms.meaning: The true philosophic proportions: the one part divided into two, with three parts added to each. The operator adds his weights to nature's weights.

equivalences.quote: the two third waters are the Weights of the Wise
the true philosophic proportions called also by Hermes the Weights of the Wise

terms.meaning: One ingredient in Hermes' recipe. According to the Scholiast, it and the other recipe terms signify only the sevenfold distillation of the spirit.

equivalences.quote: the Meridian Redness, that is the soul of gold

terms.meaning: One ingredient in Hermes' recipe. The Scholiast glosses it collectively with the others as the sevenfold distillation.

quotes.text: of the citrine Seyre, in like manner, half-an-ounce

terms.meaning: One ingredient in Hermes' recipe. The Scholiast glosses it collectively with the others as the sevenfold distillation.

quotes.text: of the Auripigment, half --- which are eight --- that is three ounces

terms.meaning: Drawn forth in three, with its wine perfected in thirty. The Scholiast includes it in the terms that signify the sevenfold distillation.

quotes.text: the vine of the wise is drawn forth in three, and the wine thereof is perfected in thirty

terms.meaning: The real meaning of the coded recipe: the spirit is distilled seven times, and at the eighth the fire turns it into a fire-resisting ash or subtle powder.

quotes.text: the spirit should be seven times distilled, which after the eighth distillation is converted by force of the fire into ashes

terms.meaning: The first part of the operation. It lessens the matter, dissolving it and discharging its impurities until it nears annihilation and is free of outward forms.

quotes.text: Decoction lessens the matter, but the tincture augments it
the former Hermes calls decoction, which dissolving the matter discharges also its impurities by a proper rule

terms.meaning: The continuation of the First Work. It perfects the newly formed embryo and multiplies its vivific light.

quotes.text: the Second Work, which is only, in continuation of the First, to perfect the newly informed embryo and multiply its vivific light

terms.meaning: What increases the matter (¶7). It is taken from the 'bitterness in the throat' and is the soul drawn out after the death of the first life, the red living tincture from the body. In n18 it is the self-renewing 'tincture of many dyes'.

equivalences.quote: whence the soul is ediced; which is also the red and living tincture taken from the body

quotes.text: that tincture of many dyes which, being dissolved renews itself, and dying survives itself

terms.meaning: In Hermes' text, the ethereal light: the passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven, named by analogy with the moon because its waxing and waning parallel the moon's.

equivalences.with: ethereal light / passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven
equivalences.quote: that ethereal light, which is the passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven

quotes.text: Luna after fifteen days is diminished; and in the third, she is augmented

terms.meaning: The substance in which all beings live without knowing it. It is hidden in the natural order of generation, and the enquirer must know it within himself.

quotes.text: seek to know intrinsical within themselves the substance of that Universal Nature in which they, with all beings in common, as it were, unconsciously live

terms.meaning: What is within, which must be drawn out by art and fixed.

equivalences.quote: That which is within, viz., the causal light, must be drawn forth by art and fixed

terms.meaning: What is without, which must be made flexible and hidden.

equivalences.quote: that which is without, viz., the sensual spirit of life must be made flexible and occultated

terms.meaning: The state reason must enter, after the inner light is fixed and the outer spirit made flexible, in which the powers of the Universal Nature become known from within.

quotes.text: before reason can become into that Identity by which the powers of the Universal Nature are made manifest and intrinsically understood

terms.meaning: A philosophic, fiery, vital, running substance that mixes with all metals and separates from them. It is prepared and coagulated in the innermost chamber of life and is the residue of the philosophic earth after separation. Burnt to ashes by its own fire, it generates the Stone and is born of it.

equivalences.quote: for that is Mercury which is spoken of concerning the residual earth
this argent vive, then, which is the residuum of the philosophic earth after the separation

quotes.text: Our Mercury, says the wise Scholiast, is philosophic, fiery, vital, running

terms.meaning: The water or mercury's own active principle. 'Triple sulfur' appears in the instruction about weights.

equivalences.quote: its own good sulfur, or vital flame

terms.meaning: The newborn quintessential spirit (Proteus): the Spirit of life in its active, devouring state; the first sublimed quintessence, not yet perfected. It is the same thing as the crow.

equivalences.quote: The vulture, according to our Scholiast, is the new born quintessential spirit or Proteus
The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate.

quotes.text: The vulture is the first sublimed quintessence not yet perfected by art

terms.meaning: The chief principle of the art (Hermes). It is the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state, belonging to the beginning of the work in which the revived spirit unites with its solar ferment.

equivalences.quote: the chief principle of the art is the Crow

quotes.text: when it lies in a more obscured and passive condition, the crow

terms.meaning: Another name for the newborn quintessential spirit (the vulture). Democritus' 'fable of Proteus' alludes to the matter restoring itself by an inborn force.

equivalences.quote: the new born quintessential spirit or Proteus

terms.meaning: What the revived spirit unites with in the early (crow) stage of the work. It is not otherwise explained.

quotes.text: the revivified spirit is united with its solar ferment

terms.meaning: The decay of the spirit, signified by the night's blackness. Its opposite is the resurrection, signified by the clearness of day.

equivalences.quote: The blackness of the night is the putrefaction of the same

terms.meaning: What carries the volatile spirit (crow) so that it 'flies without wings'.

quotes.text: IT flies without wings, being borne and carried by the fixed spirit

terms.meaning: The philosophic matter in its concrete form, a true mineral petrification. It is a stone and no stone (spirit, soul and body), with many cover-names, signified to the wise by the one epithet 'Philosopher's Stone'. It is born in one colour, passes through many, heals, and leads from darkness to light.

equivalences.with: feminine of magnesia, hen, white spittle, volatile milk, incombustible ash
equivalences.quote: this matter I call the Stone; but it is also named the feminine of magnesia, or the hen, or the white spittle, or the volatile milk, the incombustible ash
the stone that is venerable, splendid in colour, a mind sublime, and an open sea

quotes.text: It is called a stone, say the adepts, and it a true mineral petrification
in the concrete form, and for reasons before given in part, it has been properly called the Stone

terms.meaning: Where the stone is hidden: the central motion of mineral life, where the spirit first coagulates into concrete form.

equivalences.with: central motion of the mineral life
equivalences.quote: It is hidden in the caverns of the metals; that is to say, in the central motion of the mineral life

terms.meaning: The fire the matter is put into so that its heat increases and its dryness is destroyed. Atwood defers explaining its nature, origin and 'artificial excitation'.

quotes.text: Put the matter into a moist fire, therefore, and cause it to boil in order that its heat may be augmented
Concerning the peculiar nature, origin, and artificial excitation of the philosophic fire, we may more effectively inquire hereafter.

terms.meaning: The single operation, repeated many times, that covers all the named operations. Each time, it changes and improves the matter and drives its life to full vigour. It is unlike ordinary chemical sublimation.

quotes.text: the Hermetic sublimation is said to change the matte, qualifying and meliorating each time that it succeeds

terms.meaning: Paired with the fire, these are the external and internal agents of the work, kept in the 'sea' to the end. By either of them the matter is conserved and nourished.

equivalences.quote: By the fire and heavenly bird are dignified, says the scholiast, the external and internal agents in the Hermetic work

terms.meaning: Used of philosophers in a special sense: they withhold the truth only from the ignorant and vicious, not from the just or wise.

quotes.text: For this reason are philosophers said to be envious; not that they grudged the truth to religious or just men

terms.meaning: The knowledge from which the unworthy must be kept, lest they misuse nature's 'powerful machine' and overturn the order of final causes.

quotes.text: these are unfit to be admitted to the Causal Knowledge

terms.meaning: The tincture freed from the central essence. It is said to prolong life and cure disease, moral indulgence and physical defects.

quotes.text: This is the elixir of Light from the central essence, so set free

ambiguities.quote: nothing is done except it be compounded
readings: As printed in Hermes: nothing is done unless it is compounded (put together).
As Atwood restates it: nothing is done unless the matter is 'decompounded' (broken down and purified).
ambiguities.basis: I.3 ¶5 has 'compounded'; I.3 n4 has 'nothing is done except that the matter be decompounded'. The footnote may be correcting the text, interpreting it, or the main text may have a misprint.

ambiguities.quote: By the fire and heavenly bird are dignified, says the scholiast, the external and internal agents in the Hermetic work
readings: Read in order: the fire = the external agent, the heavenly bird = the internal agent.
The pair as a whole means the two agents, with no one-to-one assignment.
ambiguities.basis: I.3 n16 names both pairs in parallel order but does not say which is which.

ambiguities.quote: one to two, and three to one
readings: A generative sequence: one divides into two (agent and patient), whose union yields three (body, soul, spirit), which act as one (I.3 n5).
A proportion: one part divided into two, with three parts added to each (I.3 n6, the Weights of the Wise).
ambiguities.basis: I.3 n5 and I.3 n6 each gloss the division, in different terms.

ambiguities.quote: There may noe man Mercury mortify, But it be with his brother’s knowledging.
readings: The work literally needs a second person (a partner or 'brother').
'Brother' stands for some complementary agent or principle; the text says only that the reasons are 'hereafter explicable'.
ambiguities.basis: I.3 n17: 'no man, for reasons hereafter explicable, can operate the Hermetic artifice alone'; the same note stresses friendship and reciprocity, which favours a personal reading but does not settle it.

ambiguities.quote: The consummate union of the purified spirit with its course
readings: As printed: union of the spirit with its 'course' (its path or progress).
A misprint for 'source': union with its origin, consistent with 'from the central essence' in the same note.
ambiguities.basis: I.3 n18; the chunk contains many evident misprints (e.g. 'matte', 'poser', 'ediced'), but nothing in the text confirms the emendation.

ambiguities.quote: I am the White of the Black, and the Red of the White, and the Citrine of the Red
readings: A temporal order of colour stages: black, then white, then red, then citrine.
Each colour is hidden in or comes out of the one before, without a strict sequence of stages.
ambiguities.basis: I.3 ¶9; I.3 n12 pairs night/putrefaction with day/resurrection (black before clearer); I.3 n5 speaks of red and white spirits from one water. The chunk gives no explicit order.

ambiguities.quote: Put the matter into a moist fire
readings: A literal humid heat applied to the matter.
A veiled agent (the 'philosophic fire'), whose nature Atwood defers explaining.
ambiguities.basis: I.3 ¶10; I.3 n14 defers 'the peculiar nature, origin, and artificial excitation of the philosophic fire'; I.3 n16 calls the fire an agent of the work.

translations.original: non corporaliter, as the Scholiast explains, sed spiritualiter et sapienter
translations.translation: not corporally but spiritually and wisely
a mind sublime, and an open sea

translations.original: Si lapis proprium nomen haberet lapis esset nomen ejus
translations.translation: If the stone had its proper name, 'stone' would be its name.

translations.original: Juro tibi supra animaam meam quod si ea reveles, damnatus es: nam a Deo on=mne procedit bonum et ei soli debetur. Quare servabis et secretum tenebis illud quod ei debetur revelandum, etc.
translations.translation: I swear to you upon my soul that if you reveal these things you are damned: for all good proceeds from God and is owed to Him alone. Therefore you shall keep and hold secret that which is His to reveal, etc.

translations.original: Montis in excelso consistit vertice vultur, Assidue clamans, Albus ego atque niger, Citrinus, rubeusque feror nil mentior: idem est Corvus, qui pennies absque volare solet Nocte tenebrosa emediaque in luce diei Namque ortis caput est ille vel iste tuae
translations.translation: On the lofty summit of a mountain stands the vulture, crying without ceasing: 'White am I and black; citrine and red I am called; I lie not.' The same is the Crow, who is wont to fly without wings in the dark night and in the middle light of day; for the one or the other is the head of your [art]. (The Latin has apparent misprints, e.g. 'pennies', 'emediaque', 'ortis'; rendering is tentative.)

translations.original: If one evil man had hereof his will, All Christian peace he might easily spill; And with his pride he might pul down Rightful Kings and Princes of renown. Wherefore the sentence of peril and jeopardy Upon the teacher reseth dreadfully.
translations.translation: If one evil man had his will of this, he could easily destroy all Christian peace, and in his pride pull down rightful kings and renowned princes. Therefore the sentence of peril and danger rests dreadfully upon the teacher.

translations.original: He sayeth right thus withouten any lye There may noe man Mercury mortify, But it be with his brother’s knowledging.
translations.translation: He says exactly this, without any lie: no man may mortify Mercury except with his brother's knowledge.

threads.note: The treatise is 'In Seven Sections'; this chunk covers Section First, and the remaining sections follow.

'as was explained in the theory concerning other gross elementary bodies' refers to an earlier explanation that bodies reveal their true original only when reduced into it. Atwood also says 'intending to enlarge inquiry on this head, we defer our comments' on knowing the Universal Nature within oneself.
'We, also, intending to explore the Intellectual Ground more fully hereafter' is a promised later treatment.
'Concerning the peculiar nature, origin, and artificial excitation of the philosophic fire, we may more effectively inquire hereafter' defers the explanation of the philosophic fire.
The Stone is so called 'for reasons before given in part', pointing to an earlier discussion of why the matter is called the Stone.
'no man, for reasons hereafter explicable, can operate the Hermetic artifice alone' promises a later explanation of why the work needs more than one person.
